data.title: When a team is too big
data.author: gpi
data.article_summary: 文章探讨了团队规模过大带来的问题以及如何提高生产力。作者通过自身经历讲述了一个14人团队在沟通和任务分配上的低效问题，如站会无聊、信息遗漏和“幽灵任务”等。为解决这些问题，团队尝试了异步站会，但效果不佳，因为缺乏必要的对话和沟通。最终，通过将团队按技术领域划分为前端和后端两个小组，提升了效率和相关性。文章强调，通才团队能减少内部依赖和单点故障，但通才模式也有挑战。关键在于创造一个有利于持续改进的环境，而非依赖某个“万能”解决方案。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：团队在敏捷开发中的每日站会（standup）的效率、组织结构、团队角色分工以及如何处理团队扩展中的问题。

不同观点：
• Etheryte认为，站会时间过长是因为缺乏有效的引导和纪律，站会应限制在每人一分钟内，后续讨论应私下进行。Etheryte还提到瑞典文化中的非对抗性可能导致会议无法有效控制时间。
• Teeray则强调站会的核心价值在于讨论障碍和合作机会，认为如果等到站会才提出障碍问题，可能已经太迟，提倡通过即时通讯工具更快地解决问题。
• Madaxe_again指出团队规模扩大后会出现办公室政治问题，建议通过任务导向的轮换团队来打破权力斗争和内耗现象。
• Ivan_gammel将站会问题归因于中层管理缺乏经验，建议通过建立小型团队、保持专家角色和水平组织结构来解决问题，强调过程应该服务于人，而不是让人适应过程。
• Frollogaston分享了他们尝试通过指定负责人和可选会议来解决站会过长的问题，但最终发现即时召集必要人员开短会更有效。
• Bobek建议使用书面/异步站会，认为这可以避免报告的随意性，并提供了一个参考链接。
• Protocolture通过数据分析支持小团队管理的高效性，指出6人左右的团队能取得更好的管理效果。
• Pards对文章中禁止用于AI训练的声明表示兴趣，并质疑其法律效力。
• Abhaynayar表达了对从安全领域转向更广泛的技术角色的担忧，并寻求建议。
• Agge以幽默的方式回应文章中提到的“11个工程师可以吃两份披萨”，指出瑞典披萨的份量问题，并认为3-4人的团队规模更合适。
• Theptip认为全能型人才（generalist）并不是普适的解决方案，主张通过用户故事框架来报告进展，并强调团队协作和沟通的纪律性。
• Makeitdouble认为在许多公司中，业务执行比技术知识更重要，因此全能型团队能取得不错的效果，但随着公司发展，逐步推动专业化可能会带来更好的结果。
• Spenrose批评某些文章标题吸引眼球但缺乏新意，建议阅读更有深度的书籍，如《Team Topologies》。
• Mettamage认为全栈开发是解决方案，并质疑文章对跨领域学习的困难性描述，认为有CS教育背景的开发者应有能力学习不同领域的知识。
• Gwbas1c分享了自己在客户端和服务器团队分开的项目中的经验，认为过早打破团队界限不一定合适，但承认在项目早期保持全能型人才可能更有帮助。

补充讨论：

Lately I’ve been thinking a lot about these questions:
What is a team?
How large is too large and how small is too small?
What qualifies a missions?
How to weigh the cons and pros of specialist vs generalist in the age of GenAI?
There’s a story for several years back that keeps back to my mind. What makes it interesting is the fact that there was no master plan. Yet with a few cultural elements, the story took such an interesting trajectory that it shaped my leadership model. Ever since, I have been an advocate of continuous improvement by preparing the environment instead of being the wise-ass who has the ultimate solution to all problems.
Today I want to tell that story with these key takeaways:
A generalist team is less likely to have internal dependencies acting as bottlenecks, blockage, and single point of failure. Generalist teams are more productive and resilient.
Handovers introduce the risk of misunderstanding, delay, miscommunication, and diluted accountability. Clear ownership requires knowledge, mandate, and responsibility. It’s easier to implement with generalists.
But as we’ll see generalism has its own challenges as well.
Subscribe
🤖🚫 Note: No generative AI was used to create this content (except one image that’s clearly marked). This page is only intended for human consumption and is NOT allowed to be used for machine training including but not limited to LLMs. (
why
?)
Story
Many yeas ago I was part of a large team. 14 members to be exact.
The problems started from the first standup: I didn't follow 90% of what everyone else was talking about. I thought it's because I'm new to the team but as time passed and I got closer to the other team members I learned that some others feel the same.
It wasn't unusual to see someone visibly yawn or fall almost sleep during the standup. There was at least something in the round of standup that was completely irrelevant and boring to a few.
In an effort to keep the standup short, we had a time limit per person paired with invented hand gestures to signal the person who is talking that their time is over.
We were 11 engineers which can still be fed on
2-pizzas
! Size wasn't the issue.
In fact, quite the opposite: every now and then we heard about a task that never came up during the standup and wasn’t in the backlog!
We learned about those phantom tasks as they were close to the finish line or after they ere delivered.
How did that happen? Usually, someone from another team or another part of the organization reached out for a friendly
favor
and since we had enough bandwidth and great engineers, they often did their best to help.
Async Standup
Later we switch to async standup. The implementation was simple: every workday a Slack reminder would pop up with a fixed message:
What did you do yesterday?
What will you do today?
Are there any impediments or do you need any help?
Each team member would write a comment more or less in line with what they would be telling at a sync (face to face) standup.
Those comments came in during the day, and some folks consistently missed it. Regardless, I rarely read all the comments because they were not relevant to what I was doing.
This was less disruptive than taking 30 minutes (less than 3 minutes per person) for the daily standup, which often dragged to 45 minutes and sometimes even an entire hour!
The async report turned to exactly that:
a report
.
The main value of a standup is to have a dialogue about blockage and spark opportunities to work together. Otherwise, it's enough to move issues on the Kanban swim lanes with a comment. That covers the reporting part. We missed a dialogue when a dialogue was due.
Concern-based Task Forces
I raised these issue in one of our retrospectives and the EM/PM said they'll take action.
The solution they came up with was to break the team into two halves:
The front-end "task force" (as it was called) would work on front-end stuff basically taking a Figma design and turning it to working UI.
The back-end task force would cover the rest from API, to CI/CD, and configuring cloud and operations.
The idea was to have smaller groups that would move faster, delivery independently, and are more relevant and connected to each other.
And we cut the team by tech, because anyone who has worked with engineers knows that they can be quite religious about their tools of choice. Back-end/Front-end seemed to be different enough to justify that cut.
Good engineers are good problem solvers not a layer of meat wrapped around a tool!
The hypothesis was that front-end developers should care enough about each other's world and standup report. Similarly back-end
44026516.article_summary: 文章探讨了团队规模过大带来的问题以及如何提高生产力。作者通过自身经历讲述了一个14人团队在沟通和任务分配上的低效问题，如站会无聊、信息遗漏和“幽灵任务”等。为解决这些问题，团队尝试了异步站会，但效果不佳，因为缺乏必要的对话和沟通。最终，通过将团队按技术领域划分为前端和后端两个小组，提升了效率和相关性。文章强调，通才团队能减少内部依赖和单点故障，但通才模式也有挑战。关键在于创造一个有利于持续改进的环境，而非依赖某个“万能”解决方案。

data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：理查德·加尔文（Richard Garwin）的生平成就及其参与的核武与科技发展

不同观点：
• **加尔文的科技贡献**：
   - jasonhong 强调加尔文在IBM期间对多种技术（如磁共振成像、触摸屏、激光打印机等）的贡献，并提到他在23岁时设计了第一个成功的氢弹。
   - Hilift 补充了加尔文与曼哈顿计划时期其他人物（如Theodore Hall）的背景对比，指出两人都是物理学神童，且Hall曾向苏联提供核武情报。

• **加尔文的核武角色**：
   - Supermancho 对加尔文设计的氢弹威力提出质疑，引用数据称某版本的氢弹威力相当于超过60万颗广岛原子弹，但冷战分析家认为其只能摧毁一个如法国大小的区域，质疑是否因为未考虑到的因素如气压导致判断误差。

• **加尔文的和平贡献**：
   - smartbit 指出加尔文不仅是Pugwash会议的成员，还参与了多个国际科学会议，并与苏联科学家合作，致力于限制核武和太空武器的提案。

补充讨论：
• **Theodore Hall 的背景与加尔文的比较**：
   - Hilift 详细描述了Theodore Hall的背景，包括他在曼哈顿计划中的角色、向苏联提供情报以及在麦卡锡时代的反间谍调查中被保护的经历，以此与加尔文进行隐含对比。

争议焦点：
• **氢弹威力的实际效果**：
   - Supermancho 质疑早期氢弹设计的实际摧毁能力是否如当时分析家所言，提出了关于物理限制（如气压）是否影响氢弹威力的问题。

以上是评论中主要观点和讨论要点的总结。

data.title: Show HN: Defuddle, an HTML-to-Markdown alternative to Readability
data.author: kepano
data.article_summary:
Defuddle 是一个用于从网页中提取主要内容的工具，能够去除评论、侧边栏、页眉、页脚等非必要元素，使页面更易读。它旨在输出干净一致的 HTML 文档，特别适合作为 Obsidian Web Clipper 的HTML-to-Markdown转换输入。与Mozilla Readability相比，Defuddle更宽容，保留更多元素，并使用页面的移动样式来猜测不必要的部分，同时提取更多元数据。

主要功能包括：
- 安装：通过 npm 安装，Node.js 环境还需安装 JSDOM。
- 使用：可在浏览器和 Node.js 环境中使用，返回包含文章作者、标题、内容、元数据等信息的对象。
- 选项：支持调试模式、Markdown 转换、选择性删除元素等。

Defuddle 提供核心包、完整包和 Node.js 包，核心包适用于大多数场景，完整包增加数学公式处理功能。

de·​fud·dle /diˈfʌdl/
transitive verb
to remove unnecessary elements from a web page, and make it easily readable.
Beware! Defuddle is very much a work in progress!
Defuddle extracts the main content from web pages. It cleans up web pages by removing clutter like comments, sidebars, headers, footers, and other non-essential elements, leaving only the primary content.
Try the Defuddle Playground →
Features
Defuddle aims to output clean and consistent HTML documents. It was written for
Obsidian Web Clipper
with the goal of creating a more useful input for HTML-to-Markdown converters like
Turndown
.
Defuddle can be used as a replacement for
Mozilla Readability
with a few differences:
More forgiving, removes fewer uncertain elements.
Provides a consistent output for footnotes, math, code blocks, etc.
Uses a page's mobile styles to guess at unnecessary elements.
Extracts more metadata from the page, including schema.org data.
Installation
npm install defuddle
For Node.js usage, you'll also need to install JSDOM:
npm install jsdom

Defuddle 是一个用于从网页中提取主要内容的工具，能够去除评论、侧边栏、页眉、页脚等非必要元素，使页面更易读。它旨在输出干净一致的 HTML 文档，特别适合作为 Obsidian Web Clipper 的HTML-to-Markdown转换输入。与Mozilla Readability相比，Defuddle更宽容，保留更多元素，并使用页面的移动样式来猜测不必要的部分，同时提取更多元数据。

主要功能包括：
- 安装：通过 npm 安装，Node.js 环境还需安装 JSDOM。
- 使用：可在浏览器和 Node.js 环境中使用，返回包含文章作者、标题、内容、元数据等信息的对象。
- 选项：支持调试模式、Markdown 转换、选择性删除元素等。

Defuddle 提供核心包、完整包和 Node.js 包，核心包适用于大多数场景，完整包增加数学公式处理功能。

data.title: Gemini Diffusion
data.author: mdp2021
data.article_summary: Google在I/O大会上发布了Gemini Diffusion，这是其首个使用扩散模型（而非传统的自回归方法）的大语言模型。扩散模型通过逐步优化噪声生成输出，而非直接预测文本，从而实现更快的速度和更高的质量。相较于一次生成一个词的传统模型，Gemini Diffusion能快速迭代和纠错，特别擅长编辑任务，如数学和代码处理。其生成速度高达857 tokens/秒，性能号称达到Gemini 2.0 Flash-Lite的水平，且速度是其5倍。扩散模型并非完全取代Transformer，而是替代自回归机制，仍可能使用Transformer进行处理。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：谷歌发布的使用扩散技术的语言模型及其潜在应用和争议

不同观点：
• [cztomsik] 认为扩散模型可能通过后期训练实现，并提到RWKV团队用WKV替代了注意力机制，暗示FFN（前馈神经网络）可能包含了大部分有用的知识，而注意力机制本身并非那么独特或重要。他还提到固定嵌入和注意力可能加速模型训练。
• [airstrike] 对扩散模型在改进现有内容方面的能力表示怀疑，认为模型缺乏“机构知识”，即无法知道什么不在代码库中，因此在处理大型代码库时，熟悉该代码库的开发者可能比模型更有优势。
• [shreezus] 对扩散模型在代码生成中的应用感到惊讶，并期待在扩散领域看到更多进展，特别是在混合模型方面。
• [heliophobicdude] 强调扩散模型在拼写检查、代码修改和编辑器中的应用潜力，特别是其快速和精准的文本编辑功能。
• [mountainriver] 指出扩散模型在推理和规划方面的优势，因为它们可以编辑且不受早期token偏见的影响。
• [hiimshort] 关注扩散技术在低端硬件上的表现，期望其能重新平衡密度与连贯性之间的关系，使较小模型也能生成连贯文本，同时提高速度。
• [huevosabio] 对扩散语言模型在游戏机制中的应用感到兴奋，但受限于硬件，希望获得API访问权限以进行实验。
• [EGreg] 对扩散模型如何在不知道单词数量的情况下生成文本表示怀疑，认为这可能导致早期预测的token数量与实际需求不匹配。
• [findingMeaning] 提到模型的快速性和易受提示注入攻击的缺点，但总体上对模型表现持积极态度。
• [albertzeyer] 纠正关于谷歌使用扩散模型替代Transformer的误解，指出Transformer在离散扩散语言模型中仍是标准配置，并讨论了编码器-解码器模型的区别和训练细节。
• [nodja] 认为扩散模型的速度优势可能导致GPU始终在高负荷工作，但对批处理的计算节省有限。
• [renjimen] 预测扩散模型的速度将使软件开发变得更加流畅，应用可以以最小规模发布并在用户需求下扩展。
• [seydor] 对通过去除噪声生成文本的概念感到深刻，认为语言学家会对近年来发生的这些进展感到惊讶。
• [Tostino] 提出将扩散模型整合到标准自回归LLM的采样器中，以检测和纠正后验推理，并允许在生成过程中进行轻微回溯和调整。

补充讨论：
• 争议焦点：扩散模型是否能在改进大型预存内容上超越传统模型，以及其在生成文本时的token预测和数量确定问题。
• 其他值得注意的讨论点：扩散模型的速度和编辑能力在实际应用中的潜力，如拼写检查和代码修改；模型在低端硬件上的表现及其可能的应用场景，如游戏开发。

44057820.article_content:
Simon Willison’s Weblog
Subscribe
Gemini Diffusion
. Another of the announcements from Google I/O yesterday was Gemini Diffusion, Google's first LLM to use diffusion (similar to image models like Imagen and Stable Diffusion) in place of transformers.
Google describe it like this:
Traditional autoregressive language models generate text one word – or token – at a time. This sequential process can be slow, and limit the quality and coherence of the output.
Diffusion models work differently. Instead of predicting text directly, they learn to generate outputs by refining noise, step-by-step. This means they can iterate on a solution very quickly and error correct during the generation process. This helps them excel at tasks like editing, including in the context of math and code.
The key feature then is
speed
. I made it through the waitlist and tried it out just now and
wow
, they are not kidding about it being fast.
In this video I prompt it with "Build a simulated chat app" and it responds at 857 tokens/second, resulting in an interactive HTML+JavaScript page (embedded in the chat tool, Claude Artifacts style) within single digit seconds.
The performance feels similar to
the Cerebras Coder tool
, which used Cerebras to run Llama3.1-70b at around 2,000 tokens/second.
How good is the model? I've not seen any independent benchmarks yet, but Google's landing page for it promises "the performance of Gemini 2.0 Flash-Lite at 5x the speed" so presumably they think it's comparable to Gemini 2.0 Flash-Lite, one of their least expensive models.
Prior to this the only commercial grade diffusion model I've encountered is
Inception Mercury
back in February this year.
Update
: a correction from
synapsomorphy on Hacker News
:
Diffusion isn't in place of transformers, it's in place of autoregression. Prior diffusion LLMs like
Mercury
still use a transformer, but there's no causal masking, so the entire input is processed all at once and the output generation is obviously different. I very strongly suspect this is also using a transformer.
nvtop
provided this explanation
:
Despite the name, diffusion LMs have little to do with image diffusion and are much closer to BERT and old good masked language modeling. Recall how BERT is trained:
Take a full sentence ("the cat sat on the mat")
Replace 15% of tokens with a [MASK] token ("the cat [MASK] on [MASK] mat")
Make the Transformer predict tokens at masked positions. It does it in parallel, via a single inference step.
Now, diffusion LMs take this idea further. BERT can recover 15% of masked tokens ("noise"), but why stop here. Let's train a model to recover texts with 30%, 50%, 90%, 100% of masked tokens.
Once you've trained that, in order to generate something from scratch, you start by feeding the model all [MASK]s. It will generate you mostly gibberish, but you can take some tokens (let's say, 10%) at random positions and assume that these tokens are generated ("final"). Next, you run another iteration of inference, this time input having 90% of masks and 10% of "final" tokens. Again, you mark 10% of new tokens as final. Continue, and in 10 steps you'll have generated a whole sequence. This is a core idea behind diffusion language models. [...]
Posted
21st May 2025
at 9:44 pm

data.title: Silly job interview questions in Haskell
data.author: behnamoh
data.article_summary: 本文介绍了几个常见的面试问题在Haskell中的实现方法。首先讨论了回文判断函数`isPalindrome`，其核心逻辑非常直观，即比较字符串与其反转是否相同。接着演示了经典的Fizz Buzz问题，通过定义辅助函数`fizzle`来处理不同的条件判断，并使用高阶函数`for_`实现循环输出。然后分析了一个较少见的问题，即找出列表中三个数之和等于指定值的所有组合。文章展示了如何通过递归实现组合生成，并利用过滤器获取符合条件的组合。总体展示了Haskell函数式编程的简洁性和强大表达能力。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：Haskell在面试或编程任务中的使用及其优缺点

不同观点：
• [sshine] 认为使用Haskell进行面试编程很有趣，因为面试官通常不理解这种范式。他提到通过使用QuickCheck的Gen可以快速实现一个密码生成器，而不需要明确地定义单一函数，展示了Haskell在某些情况下能简化开发过程。

• [djtango] 指出Haskell在处理某些简单任务（如文件操作和CSV解析）时变得复杂，而在处理复杂任务时却显得简单，这显示了Haskell在不同类型任务上的不平衡。

• [pentaphobe] 对阅读不同编程范式的代码表示欣赏，但也提到如果在面试中遇到类似回文问题，期望候选人能提出更复杂的解决方案，而不仅仅是使用内建的`reverse`函数。

• [thdhhghgbhy] 批评Haskell帖子通常不提及算法解决方案的顺序或效率，并指出在面试中，面试官会关注如何改进初步解决方案的效率，比如回文问题。

• [lynx97] 认为一个fizzbuzz的实现例子不够好，因为检查条件两次是不必要的，建议使用where子句定义fizz和buzz以提高代码可读性。

• [ReDress] 不认为这些面试问题很傻，反而觉得它们看起来很简单，质疑为什么其他人称之为傻。

• [pensatoio] 经过十五年的职业生涯，意识到像Haskell这样的“表达性”语言实际上难以阅读。

44069289.article_content:
Today I thought it'd be fun to take a look at a few common &
simple "interview questions" in Haskell. These sorts of questions are
often used to establish whether someone has programming and problem
solving skills, and I thought it might be useful for folks to see how
they play out in Haskell since our beloved language's solutions tend to
follow a different paradigm than most other languages do. I'll withhold
any judgement on whether these questions are in any way helpful in
determining programming skill whatsoever 😅; please don't @ me about
it.
Palindromes
Let's start off nice and easy with the standard "is it a palindrome"
question! The task is to write a function which determines whether a
given string is a palindrome (i.e. whether it reads the same in both
reverse and forwards)
isPalindrome ::
String
->
Bool
isPalindrome str
=
str
==
reverse
str
>>>
isPalindrome
"racecar"
True
>>>
isPalindrome
"hello world!"
False
That'll do it! Not much to say about this one, it's nice that our
definition roughly matches an English sentence describing the problem
"does a given string equal itself in reverse". I'll leave it as an
exercise for the reader to expand it to handle differences in
capitalization however you like.
Fizz Buzz
Next up is the infamous Fizz Buzz! For the 3 of you who are
unfamiliar, for each number from 1 to 100 we need to print out "Fizz" if
it's divisible by 3, "Buzz" if it's divisible by 5, and "Fizz Buzz" if
it's divisible by both 3 AND 5! Otherwise we print the number
itself.
Let's see it!
import
Data.Foldable
fizzle ::
Int
->
String
fizzle n
|
n
`mod`
3
==
0
&&
n
`mod`
5
==
0
=
"Fizz Buzz!"
|
n
`mod`
3
==
0
=
"Fizz!"
|
n
`mod`
5
==
0
=
"Buzz!"
|
otherwise
=
show
n
main ::
IO
()
main
=
do
for_ [
1
..
100
] (
putStrLn
.
fizzle)
>>>
main
1
2
Fizz
!
4
Buzz
!
Fizz
!
7
8
Fizz
!
Buzz
!
11
Fizz
!
13
14
Fizz
Buzz
!
16
-- ...you get the idea
I write a helper function "fizzle" here which converts a number into
its appropriate string so I can keep the "printing" logic separate,
which is good programming style in Haskell as it makes things easier to
both test and reason about.
We can see that "case analysis" is very helpful for these sorts of
problems, I'm using "pattern guards" to do a sort of multi-way if
statement. Since "divisible by both 3 & 5" overlaps with the other
conditions and also is the most restrictive, we check for that one
first, then check the other two cases falling back on returning the
string version of the number itself. It all works beautifully!
I really enjoy looking at this problem as an example of how Haskell
is different from other languages. Most things in Haskell are
functions
, even our loops are just higher-order functions! The
nice thing about that is that functions are
composable
and have
very clean boundaries, which means we don't need to intermingle the
syntax
of a
for-loop
with our logic.
It's these same principles which allow us to easily separate our
effectful
printing logic from our function which computes the
output string.
The next difference we can see is that we use pattern-matching,
specifically "pattern guards", which allow us to select which definition
of a function we want to use. It looks a bit like a glorified
if-statement, but I find it's less syntactic noise once you get used to
it, and there are many more things pattern guards can do!
All that's left is to loop over all the numbers and print them out
one by one, which is a snap thanks to the
for_
function!
Next!
Sum up to N problem
Here's a less-common problem that nonetheless I've still heard a few
times! I think it was in one of my algorithms assignments back in the
day...
The task is to take a
list of numbers
and find any
combinations of
3
numbers
which add up to a

data.title: Kotlin-Lsp: Kotlin Language Server and Plugin for Visual Studio Code
data.author: todsacerdoti
data.article_summary: Kotlin语言服务器（Kotlin LSP）为Visual Studio Code提供了初步的Kotlin支持，基于IntelliJ IDEA和Kotlin插件，目前处于预先测试（pre-alpha）阶段。该项目支持JVM Kotlin Gradle项目的导入、语义高亮、导航、代码操作、重构、代码补全和格式化等功能，但仅支持JVM项目，且功能仍在快速开发和变更中，稳定性无法保证，适合实验和反馈。当前主要在macOS和Linux上的Visual Studio Code中测试通过，其他LSP兼容编辑器需手动配置。部分源码暂时未开源，待功能稳定后将完全开放。用户可通过GitHub提交问题和反馈。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：JetBrains 为 Kotlin 提供官方语言服务器支持的影响和各方观点

不同观点：
• **eitland**：尽管喜欢 Kotlin，但由于选择 Kotlin 似乎会锁定用户使用 IntelliJ，这使他犹豫是否无保留地推荐 Kotlin。他个人更喜欢其他免费的 Java IDE，尽管承认这是个人偏好，且大多数人可能不这么认为。

• **travisgriggs**：认为 Kotlin 有通用的语言服务器是值得赞赏的，但个人更喜欢在 AndroidStudio 中使用 Kotlin。VSCode 仅在没有更好选择时使用。不同的编程语言和任务使用不同的 IDE 是重要的，因为每个 IDE 都是为特定任务优化的，VSCode 更像是一个多功能工具，适合在没有专用工具的情况下使用。

• **matthew-craig**：认为 Kotlin 无法在 emacs 中使用是一个障碍，希望 JetBrains 推出 Java LSP，并表示愿意为这样的功能付费。

• **directstar2**：对 JetBrains 突然改变策略感到好奇，因为他们之前一直坚持将 Kotlin 锁定在 JetBrains IDE 中以保持竞争优势。

• **andy800**：欢迎 JetBrains 将 Kotlin 带到更多开发者使用的平台，认为 Kotlin 是其使用过的最有效率的语言，但需要一些努力才能充分利用其特性。

• **flykespice**：认为 JetBrains 支持 VSCode 是迈出了重要的一步，但对其长期可持续性持怀疑态度，因为这可能会与他们的主要产品 IntelliJ 竞争。

• **pjmlp**：质疑 JetBrains 是否会像之前对 Eclipse 插件那样在一年后取消对 Kotlin 语言服务器的支持。

• **sureglymop**：对 JetBrains 意识到需要提供官方语言服务器表示高兴。

• **misja111**：质疑为什么有人会想在 VSCode 中使用 Kotlin，认为由 Kotlin 创造者提供的 IntelliJ 是最适合 Kotlin 的 IDE。

• **jerryslm**：希望 JetBrains 也能关注 Kotlin 的 Eclipse 支持，以便在 Eclipse 中构建 Kotlin 应用。

• **twen_ty**：质疑在 Java 21/23 之后，为什么还要使用 Kotlin，特别是考虑到 Kotlin 是专有语言。

• **nsonha**：指出从 Fleet 中提取出的语言服务器可以在 Cursor 中工作，而 Fleet 本身无法加载其项目。

• **wiseowise**：对 JetBrains 终于支持 VSCode 表示兴奋。

• **mdaniel**：对部分闭源的 LSP 实现表示不满，认为 JetBrains 失去了其开源精神。

补充讨论：
• **争议焦点**：JetBrains 对 Kotlin 语言服务器部分闭源的决定引起了开发者社区的不满，部分开发者对其开源承诺产生了怀疑。

• **工具选择**：不同开发者对使用哪种 IDE 或编辑器开发 Kotlin 有不同偏好，VSCode 和其他专用 IDE 之间的选择存在争议。

• **长期支持**：有开发者担心 JetBrains 对 Kotlin 语言服务器的长期支持，特别是基于其之前对其他插件的处理经验。

Language Server for Kotlin
Pre-alpha official Kotlin support for Visual Studio Code and an implementation of
Language Server Protocol
for the Kotlin language.
The server is based on
IntelliJ IDEA
and the
IntelliJ IDEA Kotlin Plugin
implementation.
Quick Start
Download the latest build of VSC extension via
RELEASES.md
Install it as a VSC Extension via
Extensions | More Action | Install from VSIX
Alternatively, it is possible to drag-and-drop VSIX extension directly into
Extensions
tool window
Ensure that your Java version is 17 or above
Open a folder with JVM-only Kotlin Gradle project and the project will be immediately recognized and LSP activated
Supported features and Roadmap
The best way to track current capabilities and what is going to be supported in the next builds is this table:
Important note: currently, only JVM-only Kotlin Gradle projects are supported out-of-the box.
Project import
Gradle JVM project import
Gradle KMP project import
JSON-based build system agnostic import
Quickstart for JSON
Maven/Amper import
Dumb mode for no build system at all
Highlighting
Semantic highlighting
Navigation
Navigation to Kotlin (source, binary)
Navigation to Kotlin builtins
Navigation to Java (source, binary)
Code actions
Quickfixes (i.e.
replace with
)
Kotlin inspections
Organize imports
Go to reference
Refactorings
Rename
Move
Change signature
On-the-fly Kotlin diagnostics
Completion
Analysis-API based completion
IJ-based completion
Enable IJ-based completion
KDoc support
In-project documentation hovers
Dependencies/Java documentation hovers from
source.jar
Code formatting
Fully-featured Windows support
Reactive updates from the filesystem
Project Status
The project is in an experimental, pre-alpha, exploratory phase
with the intention to be productionized.
We
move fast, break things
, and explore various aspects of the seamless developer experience
including Java interoperability, limits of IntelliJ capabilities as a standalone server, native binaries of the LSP, and
debug capabilities.
The LSP supports most of the essential parts, but its final shape is not near to be defined and
even the most basic and core parts are being changed on a regular basis.
So we have the corresponding stability guarantees --
none
. It is okay to use it in your toy
projects, to experiment with it and to provide your feedback, but it is not recommended
to depend on its stability in your day-to-day work.
Supported platforms
In the current state, the golden path has been tested for Visual Studio Code with macOS and Linux platforms.
You can use Kotlin LSP with other LSP-compliant editors, but configuration must be done manually.
Please note that Kotlin LSP uses pull-based diagnostics, so the editor must support that.
You can find a standalone LSP launch script in
kotlin-lsp.sh
along
with
very experimental
(aka "works on someone's machine") instructions that setup LSP for other editors in
scripts
folder.
See
./kotlin-lsp.sh --help
for available options.
Source code
Currently, the LSP implementation is partially closed-source, primarily for the sake of development speed convenience --
it heavily depends on parts of IntelliJ, Fleet, and our distributed Bazel build that allows us to
iterate quickly and experiment much faster, cutting corners and re-using internal infrastructure where it helps.
After the initial stabilization phase and defining the final set of capabilities, we will de-couple the LSP implementation from the internal repository
and build pipelines and open source it completely (with an explicit dependency on IntelliJ), this is a temporary constraint.
VSC extension is mirrored into
kotlin-vscode
as it does not depend on anything internal.
Feedback and issues
The best way to provide your feedback or report an issue is to file a bug
in GitHub issues
.
As a temporary limitation, direct contributions are not supported as this repository is a read-only mirror,
but it is possible to open a PR into the documentation, and it will be integrated manually by maintainers.

data.title: The scientific “unit” we call the decibel
data.author: Ariarule
data.article_summary: 无法获取文章内容
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点： decibel（分贝）的使用及其在不同领域的争议和优点

不同观点：
• **lifthrasiir** 认为，任何使用分贝（bel）的情况都应该明确标注参考水平（例如dB(SPL), dB(A), dB(u)等）。每个不同的分贝单位都是独立的，仅通过它们表示对数比率这一事实相联系。对于不熟悉的分贝单位，应保持警惕。
• **fouronnes3** 指出，虽然分贝有历史遗留的缺点，但其将乘法转换为加法的特性在实际工程中非常有用，尤其是在处理极大或极小的数值时。同时，软件领域也有类似历史遗留问题但仍在使用。
• **severusdd** 认为，分贝在RF工程中非常实用，尤其是在处理信号水平和增益时，可以简化计算。尽管分贝复杂，但在当前工程实践中没有更好的替代方案。
• **etskinner** 强调，在描述声音的分贝时，测量距离非常重要，因为声压与距离的平方成反比。例如，94dB的割草机在2米外的声压会降低到91dB。
• **ggm** 提到，音频VU表的校准基于主观模型，历史上不同机构的标准不同，但这些标准后来被接受为事实标准。
• **leoedin** 支持分贝在RF和雷达工程中的使用，认为它简化了对放大器链和插入损耗的推理和计算。
• **cesaref** 认为，分贝的优点在于将增益和衰减相加而不是相乘，这在实际工作中非常方便，甚至不需要深入理解科学原理。
• **cb321** 讨论了缩写的模糊性问题，认为这种模糊性取决于读者的知识和经验，并指出有些人类喜欢使用缩写来表明内群体身份，但这会妨碍广泛沟通。
• **smat** 认为，分贝在描述比例时是有用的，但在作为单位使用时需要明确参考量，以避免混淆。
• **kristjank** 认为，抱怨分贝复杂的人可能缺乏实际工作经验，分贝在电信、RF和光纤工程中极大地简化了计算。
• **49pctber** 提供了对“普通”分贝和“带 flavor 的”分贝（如dBm）的详细解释，并指出不同类型的分贝不能直接相加，但其简化乘法为加法的特性非常有用。
• **rebolek** 认为，尽管分贝有其复杂性，但在声音工作中，它是一个足够好的表示方式，尤其是其对增益和衰减的直观表示。
• **FRidh** 指出，分贝作为相对单位，需要明确其参考量，这在实际使用中常常被忽略或错误标注，导致混乱。特别是在声压和声功率的区分上需要更加严谨。

补充讨论：
• 分贝的不同“变种”（如dB(A), dB(SPL), dBm等）及其应用场景是讨论的一个重点。明确标注参考水平和量是避免混淆的关键。
• 分贝在简化计算方面的优势（将乘法转换为加法）被多次提到，特别是在处理极大或极小数值时。
• 缩写的模糊性和历史遗留问题也被提及，这些因素增加了分贝使用的复杂性。
• 声音测量的距离因素和A加权等概念在声学工程中具有重要意义，需要正确理解和应用。

• **cb321** 讨论了缩写的模糊性问题，认为这种模糊性取决于读者的知识和经验，并指出有些人类喜欢使用缩写来表明内群体身份，但这会妨碍广泛沟通。
• **smat** 认为，分贝在描述比例时是有用的，但在作为单位使用时需要明确参考量，以避免混淆。
• **kristjank** 认为，抱怨分贝复杂的人可能缺乏实际工作经验，分贝在电信、RF和光纤工程中极大地简化了计算。
• **49pctber** 提供了对“普通”分贝和“带 flavor 的”分贝（如dBm）的详细解释，并指出不同类型的分贝不能直接相加，但其简化乘法为加法的特性非常有用。
• **rebolek** 认为，尽管分贝有其复杂性，但在声音工作中，它是一个足够好的表示方式，尤其是其对增益和衰减的直观表示。
• **FRidh** 指出，分贝作为相对单位，需要明确其参考量，这在实际使用中常常被忽略或错误标注，导致混乱。特别是在声压和声功率的区分上需要更加严谨。

补充讨论：
• 分贝的不同“变种”（如dB(A), dB(SPL), dBm等）及其应用场景是讨论的一个重点。明确标注参考水平和量是避免混淆的关键。
• 分贝在简化计算方面的优势（将乘法转换为加法）被多次提到，特别是在处理极大或极小数值时。
• 缩写的模糊性和历史遗留问题也被提及，这些因素增加了分贝使用的复杂性。
• 声音测量的距离因素和A加权等概念在声学工程中具有重要意义，需要正确理解和应用。

data.title: Good Writing
data.author: oli5679
data.article_summary: 本文探讨了优秀写作的两个方面：文字优美和观点正确，并提出两者其实是相关的。作者认为，优美的文字不仅让文章读起来更轻松，还能帮助作者发现和修正观点中的错误。通过反复修改文字，使其更流畅，作者在无意中优化了观点的表达。这种现象类似于摇晃一个装满物品的箱子，随机晃动最终会让物品更紧密地排列。此外，流畅的文字让作者作为第一个读者更容易发现问题，因为阅读起来更省力。作者进一步指出，某些词语的发音与其意义相关，优美文字的节奏也能反映观点的复杂性。因此，文字优美不仅让文章更易读，还可能让观点更正确。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：写作风格与内容正确性、思想深度之间的关系

不同观点：
• antirez认为，丰富的写作风格能够反映更深层次的思维方式，传递更多有价值的信号。他以意大利作家Giuseppe Pontiggia为例，说明优秀的写作风格能超越简单的表达，传达更深刻的含义。他认为PG的写作风格较为简单，虽然内容有价值，但风格上缺乏深度。
• jxjnskkzxxhx指出，好的写作风格并不一定意味着内容的正确性，并举例说明即使文章写得好，其中的观点也可能很愚蠢。
• idlewords用幽默的方式将PG的写作与烹饪视频相比，暗示PG的写作建议可能并不适用于所有人或所有情况。
• kristianc提到康德的哲学观点，指出语言并不能透明地传达思想，而是中介思想。他认为即使通过编辑使文章更连贯，也不一定使观点更正确。
• Waterluvian认为自信和自大可能与成功有关，但成功人士分享的意见和建议往往是这些特质的副产品，而非直接结果。
• kaushalvivek支持迭代写作可以同时提升文笔和核心观点，但他认为PG的这篇文章本身不够清晰，可以更简短。
• fogleman指出，LLM（大型语言模型）能够写出听起来合理但错误的观点，暗示好的文笔不一定意味着内容正确。
• tptacek幽默地表示，任何能让人们写第二稿评论的事情他都支持，暗示写作改进的重要性。
• luispauloml对PG文章中的两个句子感到困惑，提出了具体的问题，显示出对文章某些部分理解的困难。
• mykowebhn提到康德和黑格尔等哲学家的写作风格虽然受到批评，但他们的作品仍有长期价值，而PG的作品可能不会持久。
• rossdavidh建议通过实证测试来验证好的写作是否与内容的正确性相关，提出使用法庭证词、科学论文和股票评论等具体例子。
• MinimalAction反对文章的前提，认为好的写作风格可能只是为了操纵读者，使其相信内容正确，而不一定反映真相。
• fidotron引用法律写作的例子，指出许多法律写作在风格和内容上都有问题，认为PG将二者联系起来的尝试并不令人信服。
• Breckinloggins提到古代对“诡辩”的定义，指出为了影响力而写作可能导致内容不真实，警告作家可能无意中陷入诡辩。

补充讨论：
• 评论中多次提到PG的写作风格和内容，有人赞赏其内容但批评其风格简单，有人则对其整体写作持怀疑态度。
• 讨论中涉及哲学观点，特别是康德的语言和思想理论，以支持对写作和内容关系的不同看法。
• 实证测试和具体例子的建议显示出对理论讨论的不满，希望通过实际证据来验证观点。
• 对LLM生成内容的批评和对诡辩的警告显示出对现代写作工具和方法的担忧。

争议焦点：
• 写作风格是否能提升内容的正确性或思想深度。

• PG的写作方法和建议是否适用于所有情况或所有作家。

44081586.article_content:
May 2025
There are two senses in which writing can be good: it can
sound good, and the ideas can be right. It can have nice,
flowing sentences, and it can draw correct conclusions
about important things. It might seem as if these two
kinds of good would be unrelated, like the speed of a car
and the color it's painted. And yet I don't think they
are. I think writing that sounds good is more likely to
be right.
So here we have the most exciting kind of idea: one that
seems both preposterous and true. Let's examine it. How
can this possibly be true?
I know it's true from writing. You can't simultaneously
optimize two unrelated things; when you push one far
enough, you always end up sacrificing the other. And yet
no matter how hard I push, I never find myself having to
choose between the sentence that sounds best and the one
that expresses an idea best. If I did, it would be
frivolous to care how sentences sound. But in practice it
feels the opposite of frivolous. Fixing sentences that
sound bad seems to help get the ideas right.
[
1
]
By right I mean more than just true. Getting the ideas
right means developing them well — drawing the
conclusions that matter most, and exploring each one to
the right level of detail. So getting the ideas right is
not just a matter of saying true things, but saying the
right true things.
How could trying to make sentences sound good help you do
that? The clue to the answer is something I noticed 30
years ago when I was doing the layout for my first book.
Sometimes when you're laying out text you have bad luck.
For example, you get a section that runs one line longer
than the page. I don't know what ordinary typesetters do
in this situation, but what I did was rewrite the section
to make it a line shorter. You'd expect such an arbitrary
constraint to make the writing worse. But I found, to my
surprise, that it never did. I always ended up with
something I liked better.
I don't think this was because my writing was especially
careless. I think if you pointed to a random paragraph in
anything written by anyone and told them to make it
slightly shorter (or longer), they'd probably be able to
come up with something better.
The best analogy for this phenomenon is when you shake a
bin full of different objects. The shakes are arbitrary
motions. Or more precisely, they're not calculated to
make any two specific objects fit more closely together.
And yet repeated shaking inevitably makes the objects
discover brilliantly clever ways of packing themselves.
Gravity won't let them become less tightly packed, so any
change has to be a change for the better.
[
2
]
So it is with writing. If you have to rewrite an awkward
passage, you'll never do it in a way that makes it
less
true. You couldn't bear it, any more than gravity could
bear things floating upward. So any change in the ideas
has to be a change for the better.
It's obvious once you think about it. Writing that sounds
good is more likely to be right for the same reason that
a well-shaken bin is more likely to be tightly packed.
But there's something else going on as well. Sounding
good isn't just a random external force that leaves the
ideas in an essay better off. It actually helps you to
get them right.
The reason is that it makes the essay easier to read.
It's less work to read writing that flows well. How does
that help the writer?
Because the writer is the first
reader.
When I'm working on an essay, I spend far more
time reading than writing. I'll reread some parts 50 or
100 times, replaying the thoughts in them and asking
myself, like someone sanding a piece of wood, does
anything catch? Does anything feel wrong? And the easier
the essay is to read, the easier it is to notice if
something catches.
So yes, the two senses of good writing are connected in
at least two ways. Trying to make writing sound good
makes you fix mistakes unconsciously, and also helps you
fix them consciously; it shakes the bin of ideas, and
also makes mistakes easier to see. But now that we've
dissolved one layer of preposterousness, I can't resist
adding another. Does sounding good do more than just help
you get the ideas right? Is writing that sounds good
inherently
more likely to be right? Crazy as it may
seem, I think that's true too.
Obviously there's a connection at the level of individual
words. There are lots of words in English that sound like
what they mean, often in wonderfully subtle ways.
Glitter. Round. Scrape. Prim. Cavalcade. But the sound of
good writing depends even more on the way you put words
together, and there's a connection at that level too.
When writing sounds good, it's mostly because it has good
rhythm. But the rhythm of good writing is not the rhythm
of music, or the meter of verse. It's not so regular. If
it were, it wouldn't be good, because the rhythm of good
writing has to match the ideas in it, and ideas have all
kinds of different shapes. Sometimes they're simple and
you just state them. But other times they're more subtle

data.title: Show HN: Rotary Phone Dial Linux Kernel Driver
data.author: sephalon
data.article_summary: 该项目是一个Linux内核驱动程序，能够将旋转拨号电话转换为一个evdev输入设备。通过此驱动，用户可以将传统的旋转拨号电话接入现代计算机系统，使其作为输入设备使用。项目遵循GNU通用公共许可证v2.0或更高版本，并于2025年1月1日创建。更多详细信息可参阅项目的README文件。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：围绕老式旋转电话及其技术改造的讨论

不同观点：
• anonymousiam 分享了在 70 年代末期，他如何将 HP41C 计算器改造成一个旋转拨号电话，使用非文档化的操作码来生成拨号脉冲，并提到遇到《HP-41C Synthetic Programming Manual》一书作者的轶事。
• jtwaleson 提到将老式旋转电话改装成蓝牙耳机，并提供了相关博客和 Hackaday 文章链接，同时表示计划创建蓝牙旋转拨号键盘的替代模式。
• mauvehaus 提到在 iPhone 还是传闻时，曾建议使用类似 iPod 的触控轮来复兴旋转拨号设计，但被拒绝，因此通过设置 Linux 盒子来体验旋转拨号的感觉。
• gchamonlive 开玩笑地提到有人用旋转电话成功通关了《黑暗之魂》游戏。
• Stratoscope 分享了 30 年前与旋转电话相关的电话网络兼容性经历，并链接到相关讨论。
• kevvok 提到 Connections Museum 的工作人员编写驱动程序，使 Asterisk PBX 系统支持旧电话交换机的脉冲信号。
• jeroenhd 对最小驱动实现表示赞赏，并讨论了使用 Rust 语言重写驱动时遇到的困难和限制。
• rcakebread 提到使用 Hayes 兼容的调制解调器，可以通过 ATDP 命令用旋转拨号代替音频拨号。
• bacon_waffle 提到新西兰的旋转电话有反向的脉冲映射，即数字与脉冲数的对应关系不同。
• reaperducer 提到需要一个将旋转脉冲转换为双音多频（DTMF）信号的设备，并提到澳大利亚有人制作这样的转换器。
• CodeBeater 提到自己正在拆解和修理一个旋转电话，正好看到这篇文章，感到很巧合。

补充讨论：
• 讨论中涉及多个技术改造项目，包括将老式旋转电话与现代技术（如蓝牙、Linux 系统、PBX 系统）结合的尝试和实现方法。
• 争议的焦点并不明显，但一些评论提到了技术实现中的挑战和限制，例如 Rust 语言在驱动开发中的应用困难。
• 讨论还涉及不同国家在旋转电话技术上的差异，如新西兰的独特脉冲映射。
• 评论中分享了多个相关的技术资源和链接，为感兴趣的读者提供了进一步探索的途径。

an Architectural Time Capsule revisited in new york
The
Nakagin Capsule Tower
returns to public view this summer in a new light, as
MoMA
in New York opens an exhibition centered on its half-century lifespan. Built in
Tokyo
’s Ginza district in 1972 and dismantled in 2022, the structure was once among the clearest architectural expressions of
Metabolism
in
Japan
, a movement that sought to mirror natural growth and transformation in the built environment. Now, through a single, fully restored capsule and a constellation of archival materials, MoMA reactivates that legacy with the goal of inspiring inquiry over nostalgia.
Presented in the exhibition is capsule A1305, originally situated on the uppermost floor. For its display, it has been returned to near-original condition. Fragments of other salvaged units complete the restoration, from its modular furnishings to the audio controls and Sony color TV that defined its compact domesticity. Surrounding the capsule are more than 40 materials drawn from the tower’s five-decade history — models, promotional leaflets, film reels, and interviews that reveal how these micro-units adapted to lives far beyond their initial purpose. In a city shaped by constant renewal, this retrospective probes what it means to preserve an architectural concept.
The Many Lives of the Nakagin Capsule Tower will be on view at MoMA from July 10th, 2025 until July 12th, 2026.
Kishō Kurokawa in front of the completed Nakagin Capsule Tower, 1974. image by Tomio Ohashi
kishō Kurokawa’s Unfolding Vision
MoMA is set to exhibit The Many Lives of the Nakagin Capsule Tower as an investigation into the iconic structure, which was originally imagined by architect Kishō Kurokawa as a machine for living that could regenerate itself. While the concrete towers were to remain as infrastructural anchors, the capsules were intended to be swapped out as needs evolved. That replacement never came. Yet the life of the tower defied stillness. The
museum
’s curatorial team, led by Evangelos Kotsioris and Paula Vilaplana de Miguel, foregrounds the tower’s informal transformations — capsules turned into galleries, DJ booths, or quiet spaces of solitude — offering a portrait of architecture shaped by use that transcends its intended programming.
By acquiring capsule A1305 in 2023, MoMA ensured a rare physical survival of a building long dismissed as unmaintainable. It is one of just fourteen capsules worldwide to have been carefully reassembled in original form. Visitors will be able to experience the unit in full during selected member activations, reinforcing the tower’s original intent as a space to be inhabited. The Nakagin Capsule Tower’s presence at MoMA sits within the museum’s wider ambition to question permanence, authorship, and the mutable nature of design.
Kisho Kurokawa, Architect & Associates (Tokyo, est. 1962). Nakagin Capsule Tower, Tokyo. 1970–72. exterior view. 1972. image by Tomio Ohashi
Extending the Conversation around nakagin capsule tower
MoMA’s exhibition The Many Lives of the Nakagin Capsule Tower will extend beyond the gallery. A companion book authored by Kotsioris for the MoMA One on One series explores the structure’s life cycle, from its speculative roots to its final days. With rarely published documents and firsthand accounts from the building’s last residents, the volume deepens the narrative around this experimental habitat. A suite of programs in partnership with Japan Society will also unfold throughout the exhibition’s yearlong run, framing the project within both its original context and its new American audience.
night time at the Nakagin Capsule Tower, with Mr. Takayuki Sekine seen through the window of capsule B1004, 2016. image © Jeremie Souteyrat
Kisho Kurokawa, Architect & Associates (Tokyo, est. 1962). Capsule A1305 from the Nakagin Capsule Tower. 1970–72; restored 2022–23. data.title: The Xenon Death Flash: How a Camera Nearly Killed the Raspberry Pi 2
data.author: DamonHD
data.article_summary: 本文讲述了2015年Raspberry Pi 2被发现的一个罕见硬件漏洞：被氙气闪光灯照射时会立即关机。用户Peter Onion在论坛上报告了这一现象，引发社区广泛讨论和实验，最终确定问题是由于U16电源调节芯片采用了裸露的晶圆级芯片封装（WL-CSP），高强度光照引发光电效应，导致芯片电压调节异常。尽管临时解决方案是用Blu-Tack遮盖芯片，但长期解决方案是改进设计以防止类似问题。这一事件揭示了现代电子产品在追求小型化过程中对光学干扰的脆弱性，并提醒工程师在设计中考虑此类风险。

• itishappy指出半导体效应通常是可逆的，并讨论了光电效应在半导体中的应用，提到通过高强度光可以刺激芯片中的结点，但实际操作中效率较低。

44080533.article_content:
The Raspberry Pi 2’s vulnerability to xenon flashes became one of the most unusual hardware bugs in computing history.
Table of Contents
The Community Detective Story Begins
The Hunt for the Vulnerable Component
The Physics Behind the “Xenon Death Flash”
This Wasn’t Actually Unprecedented
The Fixes: From Blu-Tack to Better Design
What This Revealed About Modern Electronics
The Legacy of an “Adorable Bug”
Lessons for Today’s Connected World
I’ve seen plenty of weird computer bugs in my time, but nothing quite like what Peter Onion discovered in February 2015. He was proudly photographing his brand new Raspberry Pi 2 when something bizarre happenedâevery time his camera flash went off, his Pi instantly powered down.
At first, Peter thought it was just a coincidence. But after it happened three times in a row, he realized he’d stumbled onto something unprecedented.
His post to the Raspberry Pi forums
with the innocent title “Why is the PI2 camera-shy?” would soon reveal one of the strangest hardware vulnerabilities in modern computing history.
The Community Detective Story Begins
#
Peter Onion wasn’t just any userâhe was a veteran of the Raspberry Pi community and a regular at Raspberry Jams in Cambridge and Bletchley. When he reported that
taking flash photos caused his Pi 2 to crash
, the community took notice.
What happened next was like watching a crowd-sourced CSI episode unfold in real time. Forum users immediately began experimenting with different cameras and light sources. User “jdb” made a crucial discovery: his Samsung Note2 with LED flash caused no problems, but his Samsung K Zoom with a xenon flash reliably crashed the Pi 2.
This distinction between LED and xenon technology became the first major clue. The community had found their smoking gunâbut they still needed to figure out why.
The Hunt for the Vulnerable Component
#
The real detective work began when users started systematically testing which part of the Pi 2 was actually vulnerable. The initial assumption was that the main processor chip might be the culprit, but covering it with a blob of Blu-Tack (yes, really) didn’t solve the problem.
Then someone tried flipping the Pi upside down. Suddenly, it was immune to flash photography. This proved the vulnerability was purely opticalâlight had to physically reach a specific component on the board.
Through methodical testing,
the community isolated the problem to the U16 chip
âa small power supply regulator located between the USB connector and HDMI port. When they covered just this tiny component with Blu-Tack, the crashes stopped completely.
But what made this particular chip so sensitive to light?
The Physics Behind the “Xenon Death Flash”
#
The answer lay in modern semiconductor packaging. The U16 chip used something called Wafer-Level Chip Scale Packaging (WL-CSP), which is exactly what it sounds likeâ
a bare silicon die with solder balls attached directly to the circuit board
. Unlike traditional chips that are fully encapsulated in opaque plastic, WL-CSP chips prioritize miniaturization over protection.
This exposed silicon became the Pi 2’s Achilles’ heel. When hit by high-intensity light, the photoelectric effect kicked inâthe same phenomenon Einstein won a Nobel Prize for explaining.
High-energy photons striking the semiconductor created unexpected electron flows
, disrupting the voltage regulation circuitry and causing an immediate shutdown.
The intensity threshold was crucial. Regular LED camera flashes didn’t produce enough photons, but xenon flashes and laser pointers packed sufficient punch to trigger the malfunction. Even more interesting, the effect required silicon’s specific bandgap energyâmeaning infrared and visible light could potentially cause problems, but only at extreme intensities.
This Wasn’t Actually Unprecedented
#
While the Raspberry Pi incident captured headlines, similar optical interference problems had been lurking in the semiconductor industry for years.
An engineer at EDN Network revealed
that his company had encountered the exact same issue twelve years earlier with a CSP amplifier for a cell phone prototype. The phone’s own camera flash would cause the amplifier to spike when light penetrated the chip packaging.
Even more dramatic was a 1997 incident at the Haddam Neck nuclear plant in Connecticut.
A training department member took a flash photograph of a fire detection panel
, and the camera flash tricked an EPROM chip into thinking there was a fire. Within seconds, the Halon fire suppression system activated, forcing operators to abandon the control room for 35 minutes while the gas cleared.
These incidents revealed a broader truth: as semiconductors became smaller and more exposed, they also became more vulnerable to optical interference that traditional testing never considered.
The Fixes: From Blu-Tack to Better Design
#

data.title: What even is a small language model now?
data.author: yoeven
data.article_summary: 本文讨论了小语言模型定义的变化。过去，小模型可能只有几百万参数，能在手机或笔记本上运行，而如今，拥有300亿参数但只需一个GPU运行的模型也被称为“小模型”。到2025年，小模型主要分为两类：边缘优化模型（如Phi-3-mini和Gemma 2B，适合移动设备）和GPU友好模型（如Llama 3 70B，可在单个GPU上运行）。小模型的优势在于其专门化，能够在特定任务上超越通用大模型。如今，“小”更多指的是模型的可部署性、单GPU运行能力和易于调优的特性，而不仅仅是参数大小。小模型在成本和隐私方面具有重要意义，正在改变AI应用的格局。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：不同背景下“小型语言模型”的定义和分类

不同观点：
• **antirez**：根据模型运行所需的硬件资源和参数规模，将模型分为非常小、小、中、大、超大等类别。例如，非常小的模型可以在Raspberry Pi等边缘设备上运行，而超大模型则是如Gemini 2.5 PRO等最先进的大型模型。

• **zellyn**：以能运行在高端MacBook Pro上为分界线，认为接近这种大小的模型已经能执行如编码等任务。

• **armcat**：指出“小型语言模型”的定义随时间变化。过去的大型模型如BERT（1.1亿参数）在2018年被视为大型，而如今小型LLM的参数范围在3-4B左右。

• **Havoc**：认为模型大小的划分有些 arbitrary，提出以能否在3090显卡上运行为合理的分界线。

• **breckinloggins**：建议借用旧DOS内存模型的命名方式，根据运行设备的能力定义模型大小级别，如“tiny”可在微控制器上运行，“compact”可在Raspberry Pi上运行等。

• **mcswell**：质疑“小型模型”的定义，指出如果训练成本高达1万美元，是否还能算作小型模型。并提到一些小于1B参数的模型在特定任务中的应用。

• **srikz**：希望看到能在浏览器中通过WebAssembly运行的模型，理想大小在100MB以下。

• **nickpsecurity**：认为术语“小型模型”过于泛化，建议以能否在24小时内用一台A100 GPU完成训练为标准定义模型大小，并提到一些在10M-200M参数范围内的模型。

• **rickstanley**：提出是否可以有模型推荐其他适合特定机器配置的模型，例如基于Ryzen 9 6000S和RTX 3060m的笔记本电脑。

• **alexpham14**：赞赏根据实际影响和可部署性来定义“小型”模型，而不是单纯依赖参数数量。

• **GolDDranks**：认为传统Markov模型是小型语言模型的代表。

• **Dwedit**：提到“BabyLlama”模型，其参数规模在百万级别而非十亿级别。

• **stephantul**：质疑原帖是否完全由GPT-4o生成。

• **KasianFranks**：指出混合专家模型（MoE）在结合小型和大型语言模型的优势。

• **croes**：质疑大型语言模型如何能同时是小型语言模型，反映出定义上的困惑。

- 模型大小的定义随时间、硬件能力和应用场景的变化而变化。
- 训练成本和模型推荐系统成为讨论中的关注点。

44048751.article_content:
What Even Is a Small Language Model Now?
15 May 2025
Yoeven D Khemlani
Share this article
If you asked someone in 2018 what a "small model" was, they'd probably say something with a few million parameters that ran on a Raspberry Pi or your phone. Fast-forward to today, and we're calling 30B parameter models "small"—because they
only
need one GPU to run.
So yeah, the definition of "small" has changed.
Small Used to Mean... Actually Small
Back in the early days of machine learning, a "small model" might've been a decision tree or a basic neural net that could run on a laptop CPU. Think scikit-learn, not LLMs.
Then came transformers and large language models (LLMs). As these got bigger and better, anything not requiring a cluster of A100s suddenly started to feel... small by comparison.
Today, small is more about
how deployable
the model is, not just its size on paper.
Types of Small Models (By 2025 Standards)
We now have two main flavors of small language models:
1. Edge-Optimized Models
These are the kind of models you can run on mobile devices or edge hardware. They're optimized for speed, low memory, and offline use.
Examples
: Phi-3-mini (3.8B), Gemma 2B, TinyLlama (1.1B)
Use cases
: voice assistants, translation on phones, offline summarization, chatbots embedded in apps
2. GPU-Friendly Models
These still require a GPU, but just
one GPU
—not a whole rack. In this category, even 30B or 70B models can qualify as "small".
Examples
: Meta Llama 3 70B (quantized), MPT-30B
Use cases
: internal RAG pipelines, chatbot endpoints, summarizers, code assistants
The fact that you can now run a 70B model on a single 4090 and get decent throughput? That would've been science fiction a few years ago.
Specialization: The Real Power Move
One big strength of small models is that they don't need to do everything. Unlike GPT-4 or Claude that try to be general-purpose brains, small models are often
narrow and optimized
.
That gives them a few key advantages:
They stay lean
— no need to carry weights for tasks they’ll never do.
They’re more accurate in-domain
— a small legal model will outperform a general-purpose LLM on legal docs.
They’re easier to fine-tune
— less data, faster iteration.
Small models shine when you know what you want. Think: summarizing medical records, identifying security vulnerabilities, parsing invoices—stuff that doesn't need general reasoning across the internet.
30B+ Models: Still Small?
Sounds weird, but yes. The bar for what’s considered "small" keeps shifting.
With the right quantization and engineering, even a 70B model can run comfortably on a high-end consumer GPU:
Llama 3.1 70B
can be shrunk from 140GB (FP16) to 21GB (2-bit), running on a single 24GB VRAM card.
Throughput? ~60 tokens/sec — totally usable for many production workloads.
So now we talk about models being "small" if they’re:
Deployable without distributed inference
Runnable on one GPU (especially consumer-grade)
Tunable without a lab full of TPUs
It’s less about size, more about
practicality
.
Everyday Small Models: The Unsung Heroes
Not all small models are new. Some of the most widely used models today have been around for years, quietly powering everyday tools we rely on.
Google Translate
: Since 2006, it's been translating billions of words daily. In 2016, Google switched to a neural machine translation system, GNMT, which uses an encoder-decoder architecture with long short-term memory (LSTM) layers and attention mechanisms. This system, with over 160 million parameters, significantly improved translation fluency and accuracy.
AWS Textract
: This service extracts text and data from scanned documents. It's been a staple in automating document processing workflows, handling everything from invoices to medical records.
These models may not be cutting-edge by today's standards, but they've been instrumental in shaping the AI landscape and continue to serve millions daily.
Why This Matters
Small models are becoming a huge deal:
Startups
can deploy LLMs without spending six figures on infra.
Developers
can run local models for privacy-focused apps.
Enterprises
can fine-tune task-specific LLMs without massive overhead.
And when a "small model" can hold its own against GPT-3.5 in benchmarks? The game has officially changed.
TL;DR
Small models used to mean tiny. Now they mean "runs without drama."
You’ve got edge models, GPU-ready models, and everything in between.
Specialization is where small models shine.
30B and 70B models can be small—if they’re optimized well.
Practicality > parameter count.
In a world chasing ever-bigger models, small ones are quietly doing more with less—and that's exactly what makes them powerful.

主要讨论点：香港及周边地区竹脚手架的使用及其与金属脚手架的对比

不同观点：
• **竹脚手架的实用性与灵活性**：
  - [ptek] 指出竹脚手架主要用于支撑工人和防止跌落，而不是像钢制脚手架那样用于承重。竹脚手架相对轻便，适用于低层建筑，并且在高度超过45米时需要重新搭建。
  - [ddeck] 和 [RyJones] 强调竹脚手架的搭建速度和灵活性，尤其是在高层建筑外墙的临时搭建，只需少量竹竿和尼龙带即可完成。
  - [zinckiwi] 提到在台风季节，竹脚手架的轻微弹性和柔韧性使其比金属脚手架更有优势。

• **竹脚手架的安全性与标准化问题**：
  - [hunglee2] 认为竹脚手架虽然是本地优越的解决方案，但由于其有机、非标准化的特性，难以追踪、测量和量化，从而在健康和安全方面受到限制。
  - [Gathering6678] 指出竹脚手架在深圳自1994年起因安全问题被禁止使用，并认为钢材在某些情况下比竹材更便宜且更安全。

• **竹脚手架的传统与文化价值**：
  - [alexpotato] 对竹脚手架使用的绳结和绑扎技术感到好奇，并观察到简单的尼龙带和基本绳结即可有效固定结构。
  - [contingencies] 提到传统绳材料未被讨论，并指出竹脚手架在 Cantonese 剧院中的文化应用，强调其文化价值。
  - [timewizard] 批评文章对竹脚手架传统的浪漫化描述，认为在现代复杂和大规模建筑项目中，竹脚手架不再适用，且生命安全比传统更重要。

• **竹脚手架与其他地区的比较**：
  - [roncesvalles] 提到竹脚手架在印度城市也非常普遍，甚至认为这是一种印度技术。

补充讨论：
• 竹脚手架与金属脚手架在不同场景下的适用性及工人对两种材料的经验分享（如 [ptek] 的亲身经验）。
• 竹脚手架搭建过程中的具体技术细节和工具使用，如绳索、尼龙带和初始支撑结构的安装（如 [ddeck] 和 [alexpotato] 的描述）。
• 竹脚手架的文化和历史意义，特别是在 Cantonese 剧院等文化活动中的应用（如 [contingencies] 所述）。
• 竹脚手架在不同地区的法律规定和安全考量，如深圳的禁令（如 [Gathering6678] 提供的信息）。

争议焦点：
• 竹脚手架的传统价值与现代安全标准之间的冲突，特别是在大规模和复杂建筑项目中的适用性问题。

data.article_summary: "Terminator" 是一个由 AppleScript 驱动的终端会话管理工具，旨在解决 AI 编程助手（如 Cursor）在执行命令时出现挂起或无限运行导致工作流中断的问题。它通过隔离命令执行、保持开发循环的连续性、加速命令异步执行、智能终止忙碌进程以及保存会话状态来提升开发效率。开发者可以通过指定项目路径、任务标签和命令来管理终端会话，执行如新建项目、连续操作、额外任务和读取活动会话状态等操作。工具还提供模糊任务分组、进程终止协议及实时会话监控等高级功能，帮助开发者更好地控制工作流并减少中断。

🤖💥 Terminator - Terminal Session Manager
Keep Cursor, Windsurf, and other AI coding assistants working without disruption.
"I'll be back... to manage your Terminal sessions."
Mission Briefing
Terminator
is an advanced AppleScript-powered Terminal session manager designed to hunt down inefficient workflows and terminate them with extreme prejudice. This cybernetic organism solves a critical problem in AI coding assistants:
the dreaded hanging command loop break
.
The Problem: Loop Termination
When AI coding assistants like Cursor execute commands that hang or run indefinitely, they break their execution loop and become unresponsive. This forces developers to:
Manually intervene and kill processes
Restart the AI assistant
Lose context and momentum
Experience frustrating workflow interruptions
The result?
Productivity crashes harder than Skynet's network.
The Solution: Process Isolation
Terminator implements
process isolation
by running commands in separate Terminal sessions. This means:
✅
Loop Continuity
: AI assistant stays responsive even with hanging commands
✅
Faster Execution
: Commands run asynchronously in dedicated processes
✅
Better Control
: Intelligent process termination when needed
✅
Context Preservation
: Session state persists across operations
Core Directive
Just like the T-800's mission to protect, Terminator's primary objective is to
protect your development loop
by:
Creating and managing persistent Terminal sessions
Isolating command execution from AI assistant processes
Grouping related tasks by project
Intelligently interrupting busy processes when needed
Providing reliable session state management
Deployment Instructions
Training Your AI Assistant
To maximize loop performance, train your AI coding assistant (Cursor, Claude Code, etc.) to use Terminator instead of direct shell execution:
❌ Instead of this (loop-breaking):
#
Direct execution - can hang and break the loop
npm run build
✅ Use this (loop-preserving):
#
Terminator execution - keeps the loop alive
osascript terminator.scpt

The Evening was
small in the shadow of the other boats. When I arrived at the dock, it was well past midnight, and a misty rain was falling—the edge of a storm far out at sea. Mick, the captain, was blunt and salty; not old, but weathered. He led me on board and pointed down the ladder to the hull, where I immediately got into bed and fell asleep. When I woke up, Mick had gone into town, and I began to look around in the mute light of the overcast morning.
Explore the June 2025 Issue
Check out more from this issue and find your next story to read.
View More
Our plan that October was to fish for albacore off the coast of Washington State. These would be short trips—four or five days at a time—to train me up for the summer, when I’d join Mick for a real voyage. I’d taken a Coast Guard course at a community college and had my Merchant Mariner certificate, but I’d never worked on a fishing boat before. In the daylight, the Evening looked ramshackle, as if it had survived 80 years in the northern Pacific more by luck than design. I found a few photos of Mick’s family, and the Evening’s Coast Guard certificate. “Constructed 1941, 43 feet, commercial (uninspected).” On deck, fishing lines were tangled with seaweed. Scattered everywhere were about a dozen rubber doormats stamped with the words
Thankful, Grateful, and Blessed
. On a workbench stood a statue of the Virgin Mary.
We spent a few days waiting for the weather to clear. Mick did paperwork and chores and I tidied the boat. One day we took the catch he had stored in the hold’s briny ice to a cannery on a spit of land between the ocean and Grays Harbor. Water from the Chehalis River flowed into the harbor, forming a standing wave where the two bodies met. I watched a ship leaving the harbor. When it crossed the river bar, it pitched and rolled. Mick and I would be taking the same route in a few days, but the Evening was half the size of that ship, old, and made of wood. The wave looked large enough to swallow us.
That afternoon, Mick suggested that we “take her out for a little spin.” Days of stormy weather had turned the water brown. Bobbing under the surface, barely visible, were entire trees that had washed down the Chehalis. Mick made sure I knew how to use the radio, and reminded me that the Coast Guard was on Channel 16. He pointed out the white canister on one wall that held the emergency radio beacon, which would go off automatically if submerged. The life raft, he explained, would release on its own.
The forecast finally showed minimal wind, minimal swell. We’d leave Thursday, October 12, 2023, and be back Sunday or Monday. On Wednesday night, I went out for a cheeseburger and called my mom. When she asked if I was excited, I said yes.
My parents thought
I was throwing my life away. I was 27, and since graduating from the University of Virginia five years earlier, I’d been living in California, where I spent my time working at the counter of a surf shop, running cocktails to tourists on the ferry to Catalina Island, and surfing. In college, I’d talked about going to law school, or taking the Foreign Service exam. But as graduation approached, I began to look down the line at the rest of my life, and I knew I didn’t want that kind of career. I wasn’t sure I wanted any career at all.
I’d read
East of Eden
and
Barbarian Days
, and imagined California as a place where I could get far away from my East Coast upbringing, the collar-and-tie of my Episcopal-school childhood. I didn’t break the news to my parents until a week before my departure.
From the April 2025 issue: Graydon Carter on how six months working on the railroad changed his life
They said I hadn’t thought it through, that it didn’t sound like I had a plan. The lack of a plan was the point, I told them: “I’ll bus tables or whatever—I can find a job when I get there.” I could tell they thought the whole thing was ridiculous. In the end, I blew up at them. I told them I didn’t want the life they had chosen for me. I told them that they didn’t understand me, that I hadn’t asked for and didn’t want the blessings they’d given me.
After I left, I’d call home about once a month. They’d ask how I was doing; I’d tell them I was “figuring things out just fine.”
I bounced around—San Diego, Santa Cruz, Newport Beach—making friends and surfing as much as possible: daily, twice daily, sometimes all day long. But by the summer of 2023, I was restless. I would never have admitted it to my parents, but my job at the surf shop was getting old. Even surfing itself was beginning to feel rote—the same breaks, the same people, the same wave.
I wanted to get out of California, at least for a little while. I’d go to Australia for a year-long surfing bender. Maybe I’d meet some Australian girl—no, I definitely would—and never come back. I got a work visa. All I needed was

data.author: louthy

data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：Builder.ai公司的兴衰及相关争议

不同观点：
• **与Theranos或WeWork类似的案例**：nikcub将Builder.ai的兴衰与Theranos或WeWork进行类比，强调其快速崛起和崩溃的故事，并预测在AI投资热潮中会出现更多类似案例。
• **会计事务所的关联问题**：krona提到会计事务所合伙人与公司创始人的其他公司有联系，指出了潜在的利益冲突。
• **更多AI初创公司将面临资金问题**：empiko预测更多AI初创公司将面临资金枯竭的问题，特别是那些没有实际产品的公司。
• **英国公司欺诈问题的普遍性**：benbojangles指出在英国，许多公司通过夸大股价进行欺诈，并对诚信经营的企业家造成影响。
• **AI公司的高资本需求**：spamizbad认为AI公司比典型的SaaS初创公司需要更多的资本，并且运营更具挑战性。

补充讨论：
• **对AI应用的质疑**：gchamonlive对当前许多AI应用的可持续性提出质疑，认为真正有用的AI应用应能在消费级硬件上运行，而不是依赖昂贵的多百万美元设置。
• **对Builder.ai资金去向的疑惑**：zpeti对Builder.ai如何花费5亿美元表示不解，并对投资者为何未察觉问题表示惊讶。
• **对公司治理的批评**：conradfr对公司创始人保留“首席巫师”头衔表示讽刺，kwillets批评英国在公司治理方面缺乏类似Sarbanes-Oxley的法案。
• **对公司领导层和VC影响的讨论**：aaomidi认为VC的介入可能破坏公司的长期发展轨迹，导致创始人偏离最初的目标和愿景。
• **对行业整合的担忧**：xyst担心Builder.ai的崩溃只是行业内更多公司倒闭的开始，并担心大型科技公司会借机低价收购有价值的初创公司。
• **对法律和惩罚的看法**：6stringmerc强调需要更严格的法律惩罚机制来阻止不良行为者继续在企业治理中扮演角色。

争议焦点：
• **Builder.ai是否存在欺诈行为**：评论中多次提到公司可能存在欺诈和财务造假问题，特别是其资金使用和收入重述。
• **投资者责任问题**：对投资者为何未能察觉公司问题表示疑惑，并对他们的责任进行了隐含的讨论。

总结：评论主要围绕Builder.ai的崩溃展开，涉及公司治理、财务透明度、AI行业的挑战以及投资者和法律机制的责任等问题。

data.title: DumPy: NumPy except it's OK if you're dum
data.author: RebelPotato
data.article_summary: 文章讨论了NumPy在处理高维数组时的复杂性问题，并提出了一种简化的解决方案，称为"DumPy"。作者认为NumPy虽然强大，但需要用户进行过多思考，尤其是在处理数组维度时，不同函数有不同的规则，导致使用不便。作者建议回归使用类似循环和索引的语法，但实际上仍将其编译为向量化操作，从而避免手动循环的低效问题。这种方法旨在减少不必要的思考，同时保持运算速度，特别是针对GPU的优化。文章通过具体例子展示了NumPy的复杂性以及DumPy的简化潜力，强调简单直观的操作。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：Numpy的语法和使用难度，以及是否有更好的替代方案或改进方式。

不同观点：
• [the__alchemist] 认为Numpy的语法难以理解，尤其在嵌套循环和Numpy函数的对比中，嵌套循环更易理解和通用。
• [jampekka] 部分同意上述观点，但强调Numpy的广播机制使其强大和灵活，尽管广播规则可以更简单一致。同时指出使用vmap和FP在Python中受限。
• [turtletontine] 提出Numpy的einsum函数可以实现类似的功能，尽管接口不同，但也能简化复杂操作。
• [credit_guy] 不认为 loops 是好的解决方案，指出常规Numpy虽然复杂但可以处理任意形状的数组，并分享了自己使用Copilot进行向量化的经验。
• [joshjob42] 倾向使用Julia，因为其在矩阵运算和GPU支持上更优秀，并且可以通过PyCall调用Python库。
• [Gimpei] 强调高维数组操作本身就难以理解，Numpy可能可以改进，但loops不是解决方案，且Numpy语法不易读。
• [bee_rider] 对广播机制持批评态度，认为如果Numpy没有广播可能会更好，并指出某些操作应返回错误而非执行不相关操作。

补充讨论：
• [mpascale00] 希望有类似`ggplot2`的直观语法用于高维操作，并认为可以改进使数学运算更符合Python的Zen。
• [kevmo314] 对loops提案不认同，提到TensorFlow的懒惰求值导致调试困难，认为PyTorch因此胜出，并表示理解对Numpy的挫败感。
• [okigan] 认同文章中对Numpy使用中WTF时刻的解释，尽管自己不常使用Numpy。
• [bbminner] 支持新的索引和广播表示方式，并提到这种表示可能允许找到更优的低级实现，同时提到曾见过相关研究但未能找到引用。
• [shiandow] 对新语法的未来适应性表示担忧，询问是否需要持续开发以保持更新，并提出一些替代语法建议。
• [3eb7988a1663] 仅对代码字体颜色提出小抱怨。
• [duchenne] 希望Pytorch能有类似改进。
• [netbioserror] 认为这种DSL构造适合有宏的语言，如Lisp、Nim，并讨论高维数组索引和广播的理想语法。

DumPy: NumPy except it's OK if you're dum

So what’s the fix?

A tiny bit of cleverness

What I want from an array language is:
Don’t make me think.
Run fast on GPUs.
Really, do not make me think.
Do
not
.
I say NumPy misses on three of these. So I’d like to propose a “fix” that—I claim—eliminates 90% of unnecessary thinking, with no loss of power. It would also fix all the things based on NumPy, for example every machine learning library.
I know that sounds grandiose. Quite possibly you’re thinking that good-old dynomight has finally lost it. So I warn you now: My solution is utterly non-clever. If anything is clever here, it’s my single-minded rejection of cleverness.
To motivate the fix, let me give my story for how NumPy went wrong. It started as a nice little library for array operations and linear algebra. When everything has two or fewer dimensions, it’s great. But at some point, someone showed up with some higher-dimensional arrays. If loops were fast in Python, NumPy would have said, “Hello person with ≥3 dimensions, please call my ≤2 dimensional functions in a loop so I can stay nice and simple, xox, NumPy.”
But since loops are slow, NumPy instead took all the complexity that would
usually
be addressed with loops and pushed it down into individual functions. I think this was a disaster, because
every time
you see some function call like
np.func(A,B)
, you have to think:
OK, what shapes do all those arrays have?
And what does
np.func
do when it sees those shapes?
Different functions have different rules. Sometimes they’re bewildering. This means constantly thinking and constantly moving dimensions around to appease the whims of particular functions. It’s the
functions
that should be appeasing
your
whims!
Even simple-looking things like
A*B
or
A[B,C]
do quite different things depending on the starting shapes. And those starting shapes are often themselves the output of
previous
functions, so the complexity spirals.
Worst of all, if you write a new ≤2 dimensional function, then high-dimensional arrays are your problem.
You
need to decide what rules to obey, and then
you
need to re-write your function in a much more complex way to—
Voice from the back
: Python sucks! If you used a real language, loops would be fast! This problem is stupid!
That was a strong argument, ten years ago. But now everything is GPU, and GPUs hate loops. Today, array packages are cheerful interfaces that
look
like Python (or whatever) but are actually embedded languages that secretly compile everything into special GPU instructions that run on whole arrays in parallel. With big arrays, you need GPUs. So I think the speed of the host language doesn’t matter so much anymore.
Python’s slowness may have paradoxically turned out to be an
advantage
, since it forced everything to be designed to work without loops even before GPUs took over.
Still, thinking is bad, and NumPy makes me think, so
I don’t like NumPy
.
So what’s the fix?
Here’s my extremely non-clever idea: Let’s just admit that loops were better. In high dimensions, no one has yet come up with a notation that beats loops and indices. So, let’s do this:
Bring back the syntax of loops and indices.
But don’t actually
execute
the loops. Just take the syntax and secretly compile it into vectorized operations.
Also, let’s get rid of all the insanity that’s been added to NumPy because loops were slow.
That’s basically the whole idea. If you take those three bullet-points, you could probably re-derive everything I do below. I told you this wasn’t clever.

data.article_summary: 这篇文章介绍了2015年1月至4月进行的一项阅读理解能力研究，对象是来自堪萨斯两所大学的85名英语专业学生。研究采用“出声思考”法，要求学生朗读并翻译查尔斯·狄更斯《荒凉山庄》的前七段，以评估他们的阅读理解能力。学生在阅读前可使用在线资源和词典，并在无教师指导的情况下自行控制阅读进度。研究还收集了学生的个人数据并进行了全国读写能力考试。结果显示，尽管英语专业学生通常被认为能自主阅读指定文学作品，但实际阅读能力存在问题。该研究填补了大学阅读技能研究方面的空白，借鉴了前人如Haas、Flower等人的研究方法。研究旨在深入了解大学生的阅读认知过程。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：英语文学学科是否应继续强调“细读”方法，以及英语课程（如英语101）是否应归属到其他学科（如传播学）。

不同观点：
• 观点一：英语文学学科已经明显摒弃了“细读”方法以及支撑它的“新批评”理论，现在的课程内容和教学方式发生了变化。支持这一观点的人提到，英语文学研究已经转向其他理论和方法，细读不再是核心。
   
• 观点二：鉴于研究中只有38%的受试者能够被称为“合格的读者”，有人认为英语101这类必修课程应归入传播学或其他学科。这一观点的论据是，英语101课程更多是在支持英语系的生存，而这些课程的核心技能（如阅读和交流）更适合放在传播学或其他实用性更强的学科中。

补充讨论：
• 争议焦点在于英语文学教育的核心目标和方法。一部分人认为摒弃“细读”是学科发展的自然结果，而另一部分人则质疑这种转变是否有利于学生的基本技能培养。
   
• 另一个值得注意的讨论点是英语系的存在价值和课程设置的合理性，尤其是在必修课程方面。有人认为这些课程更多是为了维持英语系的运作，而非为了学生的实际需求。

总结：讨论主要集中在英语文学教育方法的转变以及英语课程的归属问题上，涉及到细读方法的存废和课程设置的合理性。

They Don’t Read Very Well:
A Study of the Reading Comprehension Skills of English Majors at Two Midwestern Universities
1
Susan Carlson
(bio)
,
Ananda Jayawardhana
(bio)
, and
Diane Miniel
(bio)
Abstract
This paper analyzes the results from a think-aloud reading study designed to test the reading comprehension skills of 85 English majors from two regional Kansas universities. From January to April of 2015, subjects participated in a recorded, twenty-minute reading session in which they were asked to read the first seven paragraphs of Charles Dickens’
Bleak House
out loud to a facilitator and then translate each sentence into plain English. Before subjects started the reading tests, they were given access to online resources and dictionaries and advised that they could also use their own cell phones as a resource. The facilitators also assured the subjects that were free to go at their own pace and did not have to finish reading all seven paragraphs by the end of the exam. As part of the study, each subject filled out a survey collecting personal data (class rank, G.P.A., etc.) and took a national literacy exam (the
Degrees of Reading Power Test 10A
). After the 85 taped reading tests were completed, the results were transcribed and coded.
English professors often assume that students can read the novels and poetry assigned for their courses. However, like many of our colleagues, we have come to question that assumption. To gain some insight, we conducted a reading test from January to April 2015 to record what happens when 85 college English majors read a literary text completely on their own, with no help from instructors or guidance from other students. Although there has been extensive research on the reading comprehension skills of K-12 and college developmental students, less attention has been paid to the reading skills of average four-year college students, and there are few think-aloud studies for this population. Overall, studies on college reading lag behind similar research on critical thinking and begin to increase in number only after 2019 (
Van 4
). We sought through our study to deepen our understanding of how college students read, based on previous studies like those by
Christina Haas and Linda Flower (1988)
,
Helen St. Clair-Thompson, et al. (2018)
, and
Kelly B. Cartwright, et al. (2020)
.
[End Page 1]
In general terms, our study was designed to test how college students create meaning while they read. For our reading sample, we chose the first seven paragraphs of Charles Dickens’ 1853 masterpiece,
Bleak House
. The first paragraph of the reading sample is stated below.
LONDON. Michaelmas term lately over, and the Lord Chancellor sitting in Lincoln’s Inn Hall. Implacable November weather. As much mud in the streets, as if the waters had but newly retired from the face of the earth, and it would not be wonderful to meet a Megalosaurus, forty feet long or so, waddling like an elephantine lizard up Holborn Hill. Smoke lowering down from chimney-pots, making a soft black drizzle with flakes of soot in it as big as full-grown snowflakes—gone into mourning, one might imagine, for the death of the sun. Dogs, undistinguishable in mire. Horses, scarcely better; splashed to their very blinkers. Foot passengers, jostling one another’s umbrellas, in a general infection of ill-temper, and losing their foot-hold at street-corners, where tens of thousands of other foot passengers have been slipping and sliding since the day broke (if this day ever broke), adding new deposits to the crust upon crust of mud, sticking at those points tenaciously to the pavement, and accumulating at compound interest.
(49)
Students read each sentence out loud and then interpreted the meaning in their own words—a process
Ericsson and Simon (220)
called the “think-aloud” or “talk-aloud” method. In this 1980 article, the writers defend this strategy as a valid way to gather evidence on cognitive processing. In their 2014 article for
Contemporary Education Psychology
, C. M. Bohn-Gettler and P. Kendeou further note how “These verbalizations can provide a measure of the actual cognitive processes readers engage in during comprehension” (208). data.article_summary: 这篇文章讨论了统计学中两种主要方法——频率学派和贝叶斯学派——的哲学区别和实际应用。频率学派认为概率是多次重复实验中事件发生的频率，因此不能讨论某个固定真值的概率。相反，贝叶斯学派将概率视为对某一事件的确定性程度，可以讨论真值落在某个范围的概率，反映了基于先验信息和数据的认知。文章通过一个简单的天文学光子计数问题，展示了如何用Python代码实现这两种方法，并比较了它们的实际应用。频率学派侧重于多次测量的极限情况，而贝叶斯学派则基于已有数据和先验知识进行推断。

This post is part of a 5-part series:
Part I
Part II
Part III
Part IV
Part V
See also
Frequentism and Bayesianism: A Python-driven Primer
, a peer-reviewed article partially based on this content.
One of the first things a scientist hears about statistics is that there is are two different approaches: frequentism and Bayesianism. Despite their importance, many scientific researchers never have opportunity to learn the distinctions between them and the different practical approaches that result. The purpose of this post is to synthesize the philosophical and pragmatic aspects of the frequentist and Bayesian approaches, so that scientists like myself might be better prepared to understand the types of data analysis people do.
I'll start by addressing the philosophical distinctions between the views, and from there move to discussion of how these ideas are applied in practice, with some Python code snippets demonstrating the difference between the approaches.
Frequentism vs. Bayesianism: a Philosophical Debate
¶
Fundamentally, the disagreement between frequentists and Bayesians concerns the definition of probability.
For frequentists, probability only has meaning in terms of
a limiting case of repeated measurements
. That is, if I measure the photon flux $F$ from a given star (we'll assume for now that the star's flux does not vary with time), then measure it again, then again, and so on, each time I will get a slightly different answer due to the statistical error of my measuring device. In the limit of a large number of measurements, the
frequency
of any given value indicates the probability of measuring that value.  For frequentists
probabilities are fundamentally related to frequencies of events
. This means, for example, that in a strict frequentist view, it is meaningless to talk about the probability of the
true
flux of the star: the true flux is (by definition) a single fixed value, and to talk about a frequency distribution for a fixed value is nonsense.
For Bayesians, the concept of probability is extended to cover
degrees of certainty about statements
.  Say a Bayesian claims to measure the flux $F$ of a star with some probability $P(F)$: that probability can certainly be estimated from frequencies in the limit of a large number of repeated experiments, but this is not fundamental. The probability is a statement of my knowledge of what the measurement reasult will be. For Bayesians,
probabilities are fundamentally related to our own knowledge about an event
. This means, for example, that in a Bayesian view, we can meaningfully talk about the probability that the
true
flux of a star lies in a given range.  That probability codifies our knowledge of the value based on prior information and/or available data.
The surprising thing is that this arguably subtle difference in philosophy leads, in practice, to vastly different approaches to the statistical analysis of data.  Below I will give a few practical examples of the differences in approach, along with associated Python code to demonstrate the practical aspects of the resulting methods.
Frequentist and Bayesian Approaches in Practice: Counting Photons
¶
Here we'll take a look at an extremely simple problem, and compare the frequentist and Bayesian approaches to solving it. There's necessarily a bit of mathematical formalism involved, but I won't go into too much depth or discuss too many of the subtleties. If you want to go deeper, you might consider — please excuse the shameless plug — taking a look at chapters 4-5 of
our textbook
.
The Problem: Simple Photon Counts
¶
Imagine that we point our telescope to the sky, and observe the light coming from a single star. For the time being, we'll assume that the star's true flux is constant with time, i.e. that is it has a fixed value $F_{\rm true}$ (we'll also ignore effects like sky noise and other sources of systematic error). We'll assume that we perform a series of $N$ measurements with our telescope, where the $i^{\rm th}$ measurement reports the observed photon flux $F_i$ and error $e_i$.
The question is, given this set of measurements $D = \{F_i,e_i\}$, what is our best estimate of the true flux $F_{\rm true}$?
(Gratuitous aside on measurement errors: We'll make the reasonable assumption that errors are Gaussian. In a Frequentist perspective, $e_i$ is the standard deviation of the results of a single measurement event in the limit of repetitions of *that event*. In the Bayesian perspective, $e_i$ is the standard deviation of the (Gaussian) probability distribution describing our knowledge of that particular measurement given its observed value)
Here we'll use Python to generate some toy data to demonstrate the two approaches to the problem. Because the measurements are number counts, a Poisson distribution is a good approximation to the measurement process:
In [1]:
# Generating some simple photon count data
import
numpy
as
np
from
scipy
import
stats
np
.
random
.
seed
(
1
)

44080471.article_summary: 这篇文章讨论了统计学中两种主要方法——频率学派和贝叶斯学派——的哲学区别和实际应用。频率学派认为概率是多次重复实验中事件发生的频率，因此不能讨论某个固定真值的概率。相反，贝叶斯学派将概率视为对某一事件的确定性程度，可以讨论真值落在某个范围的概率，反映了基于先验信息和数据的认知。文章通过一个简单的天文学光子计数问题，展示了如何用Python代码实现这两种方法，并比较了它们的实际应用。频率学派侧重于多次测量的极限情况，而贝叶斯学派则基于已有数据和先验知识进行推断。

44060156.article_content:
Ancient law requires a bale of straw to hang from Charing Cross rail bridge
Published on 22nd May 2025  by ianVisits in
Transport News
The scaffolding surrounding the Charing Cross railway bridge has received an addition – two bales of hay/straw – because an ancient law requires it.
The law requires a bale of straw to be hung from a bridge as a warning to mariners whenever the height between the river and the bridge’s arches is reduced, as it is at Charing Cross at the moment.
According to the Port of London Thames Byelaws, Clause 36.2, a bale of straw has to be placed under London bridges “when the headroom of an arch or span of a bridge is reduced from its usual limits”.
At night, the bale of straw is harder to see, so some warning lights are also switched on.
Quite why a bale of straw is needed has long since been lost to time, but regardless of its origins, whenever the river bylaws are updated, they keep the medieval law intact.
At the moment, what is officially the
Hungerford Bridge
into
Charing Cross station
is undergoing the first phase of several years worth of
maintenance work
, which will see one arch at a time covered in scaffolding to allow the work to be carried out.
As the scaffolding hangs below the bridge – it triggers the old law about restricted heights under a bridge, so the contractors needed to buy a couple of bales of hay/straw.
For convenience, they’re actually hanging from the Jubilee footbridges, one on either side of the railway.
At the moment, one railway arch has the bales of hay/straw as the height is restricted, although the arch is still open to river traffic. Over the next few years, the scaffolding will move northwards along the bridge, and the bale will need to move along with it.
So, for the next few years, there will be a bale of hay/straw hanging from the Charing Cross railway bridge, because an ancient law says so.
Addendum
– Although the bylaw says straw, I write hay/straw, because if I write straw, I get complaints from people claiming the bale looks like it’s hay, and if I write hay, I get complaints from people claiming the bale looks like it’s straw.
If I write both, I still get complaints, but slightly fewer.

data.title: That fractal that's been up on my wall for years
data.author: chriskw
data.article_summary: 本文讲述了作者在中学时无意间创造了一种分形图案，并将其贴在墙上长达12年。作者描述了该图案的绘制方法：从一个正方形开始，反复在上下左右复制拼贴，并交替进行一定角度的旋转。作者后来通过数学分析发现，该图案与一些已知分形（如Gosper曲线）有相似之处，但其具体生成方式与L-系统生成的“Quadratic von Koch island”略有不同。作者探讨了两种方法的差异，并尝试用不同的规则生成该独特的分形。尽管其图案与常见分形不同，但作者找到了生成该分形的规则，并进一步讨论了相关数学概念。
